ECE 6390

Product parity and a correctable error

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how row and column parity turn a small data block into a single-error-correcting code.

An even-parity check requires the XOR of its complete group to be 0. XOR is addition modulo 2: 1⊕1 = 0. Adding one parity bit detects every odd number of flips in that group, but two flips can cancel. A failed single check indicates inconsistency without locating the changed position.

The figure arranges four information bits as a 2×2 block and appends row and column parity, including a corner check. The result has nine coded bits, so code rate r = 4/9. Every row and column has even parity. With exactly one error anywhere in the 3×3 block, one failed row and one failed column intersect at the changed bit.

The adjustable model selects up to two distinct bit positions to flip. A displayed repair is justified only when the selected channel model contains exactly one error. For multiple errors, check patterns alone may be ambiguous. Four changes at a rectangle’s corners can preserve every parity check and escape detection.

This tiny product code illustrates the purpose of structured redundancy. A practical LDPC decoder has many coupled sparse constraints and soft reliability; its graph, block length and error performance require their own model. The nine-bit demonstration is not the DVB-S2 code.

Example

Data [[1, 0],[1, 1]] become [[1, 0, 1],[1, 1, 0],[0, 1, 1]]. Flip the left bit of the middle row: only that row and the first column fail. Their intersection identifies the flipped bit. The five added bits are code overhead, not additional user data.

Practice

1. If a parity-bit location rather than a data-bit location flips once, does the row/column method still locate it?

Check every row and every column, including the parity row and column.

Yes. A single flip anywhere belongs to one row and one column, so their failed checks still intersect at that position.

2. Why can four flips at a rectangle’s corners pass every check?

Count changed bits separately within each touched row and column.

Each affected row and column contains two flips, an even number. Their XOR checks therefore keep the original parity even though the data differ.
